catalog_quote: Foley (1986, p. 63) feels that, although tonal systems have been reported for a number of Papuan languages, they would “seem better anaylsed as pitch-accent systems rather than as genuine tonal systems.” We concur with this analysis. In a pitch-accent system, accented syllables are differentiated from unaccented syllables by a jump to a higher pitch. Although this pitch-accent system is not predictable, we suggest that it is probably decreasing in its function, and does not need to be written in the orthography. ... Stress in general is fairly free in its placement, rendering it basically unpredictable. There is not a clear default preference for one syllable over another one. There is one minor observable tendency that if a word ends in a heavy syllable closed by a coda consonant, then that syllable tends to attract the stress. Minimal pairs of stress patterns do exist in the language.…

new_statements.quote: In a pitch-accent system, accented syllables are differentiated from unaccented syllables by a jump to a higher pitch. Although this pitch-accent system is not predictable, we suggest that it is probably decreasing in its function, and does not need to be written in the orthography. ... Stress in general is fairly free in its placement, rendering it basically unpredictable. There is not a clear default preference for one syllable over another one. There is one minor observable tendency that if a word ends in a heavy syllable closed by a coda consonant, then that syllable tends to attract the stress. Minimal pairs of stress patterns do exist in the language. They are easily determined by context, and do not need to be marked.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (realised mainly as higher pitch, i.e. a pitch accent) is lexically free/unpredictable with no default syllable; the only tendency noted is that a word-final closed (heavy) syllable attracts stress; stress minimal pairs exist (e.g. [khabi] 'axe' vs [khabi] 'never mind'). The other first-hand source, Schieffelin & Feld 1998: xvii, gives length-based citation-form defaults instead (2-syll initial, 3-syll initial or penult, 4-syll penult; inflected forms penult; sentence-final definite-past verbs final) while also listing many unpredictable contrastive pairs.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in either source (Schieffelin & Feld describe only one 'strong' syllable per word, with particles/pronouns/kin terms 'weak' throughout).
new_statements.exceptions: G&G: final closed syllables tend to attract stress; minimal stress pairs exist. S&F 1998: definite past verbs (always sentence-final) carry final stress contrasting with homographic non-verbs (ali/alí, gulu/gulú, so:go:/so:gó:, módo:/modó:); grammatical particles, kinship terms, pronouns, loans and sound words are weak on all syllables; some pairs unpredictable (hímu/himú, hó:/ho:, ká:n/ka:n).
new_statements.domain_note: G&G statement is about the word; earlier OPD (2004) says stress is manifested by pitch not intensity/length, and both G&G and S&F treat the older 'high/low tone' reports (Rule 1964) as a stress/pitch accent contrast. S&F's patterns are explicitly for citation forms; they note sentence-final definite-past verbs get extra final-syllable stress (phrase-position effect).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Kaluli proper (kalu1248; 'Bosavi' is Schieffelin & Feld's name for the same language). Grosh & Grosh data mainly from Suguniga and Didesa villages; Schieffelin & Feld from Sululib/Bono area. No dialect split relevant to the stress statement is reported.

sources.note: Sec. 5 'Stress, Tone, and Intonation' pp. 68-69: reject Rule's 3-level tone analysis; follow Foley in treating it as pitch accent (accented syllable = jump to higher pitch), 'not predictable' and of decreasing functional load; 'Stress in general is fairly free in its placement, rendering it basically unpredictable. There is not a clear default preference for one syllable over another'; minor tendency for a word-final closed (heavy) syllable to attract stress; stress minimal pairs exist (khabi 'axe' vs 'never mind').
